content: Urticaria, commonly referred to as hives, can be classified into various types based on the way the wheals (raised, itchy skin lesions) appear. Broadly, urticaria is divided into spontaneous and physical types. Spontaneous urticaria is further categorized into acute and chronic forms, depending on the duration of symptoms. Acute urticaria lasts less than six weeks, while chronic urticaria persists for six weeks or longer. Other specific forms of urticaria include cholinergic urticaria (triggered by heat or sweating), adrenergic urticaria, aquagenic urticaria (triggered by water), contact urticaria, and drug-induced urticaria. The pathophysiology of urticaria involves complex mechanisms, many of which are still under investigation. Inflammatory processes driven by immune cell activation play a central role. Key immune cells implicated in urticaria include basophils, mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and T cells. Among these, basophils and mast cells are particularly significant, as their activation is often linked to intracellular signaling defects or autoimmune conditions. Immunoglobulin E (IgE) autoantibodies, such as IgE anti-IL-24, have been identified in patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria. The complement system also contributes to the pathogenesis, with components like C3, C4, and C5 playing a role. Genetic studies have revealed alterations in gene expression in affected skin, with upregulation of genes involved in adhesion (e.g., SELE), cell activation (e.g., CD69), and chemotaxis (e.g., CCL2). Urticaria is frequently associated with autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, as well as conditions like mastocytosis (e.g., urticaria pigmentosa), atopic diseases (e.g., atopic dermatitis, hay fever, allergic asthma), systemic lupus erythematosus, and angioedema. The causes of urticaria can be idiopathic or related to immunological disorders, including autoimmune diseases, food allergies, medications, and infections. Non-immunological triggers include physical stimuli, dietary pseudo-allergens, and hereditary factors. Differentiating urticaria from other conditions is essential for appropriate management. Differential diagnoses include hereditary or acquired complement deficiencies (e.g., C1 deficiency), cutaneous mastocytosis, malignancies, connective tissue diseases, angioedema, and exercise-induced anaphylaxis. Epidemiological data on urticaria are challenging to determine due to the transient nature of symptoms in many patients. However, studies estimate an annual incidence of approximately 0.154% and a lifetime prevalence of 12–23.5%. Urticaria can affect individuals of all ages, but it is most common in those aged 20–40 years. Women are more frequently affected than men, with an overall female-to-male ratio of 2:1.1. There is no racial predilection for urticaria. The natural history, complications, and prognosis of urticaria depend on factors such as the patient’s age, gender, urticaria subtype, and the presence of concurrent angioedema. Remission rates vary widely, with 10–60% of cases resolving within 5–10 years of diagnosis. Treatment typically alleviates symptoms in most patients. The mean duration of urticaria varies by subtype. Complications include superimposed bacterial infections, anaphylaxis, and excoriation due to intense itching. Younger patients (under 19 years) tend to have a better prognosis and treatment response compared to older adults. Factors associated with a worse prognosis include female gender, a prolonged disease course at the time of initial presentation, concurrent angioedema, certain subtypes (e.g., physical urticaria, cholinergic urticaria), and chronic use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The diagnosis of urticaria is based on clinical history, symptoms, and physical examination. Chronic urticaria persists for at least six weeks. Common symptoms include pruritus (itching) and wheals, while less common symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, and a burning sensation. On physical examination, urticaria is characterized by raised, red, itchy welts that can appear anywhere on the body, typically measuring about 5 mm in diameter. Laboratory tests can aid in assessing disease severity, treatment response, and prognosis. Diagnostic tools include the autologous serum skin test (ASST) and basophil activation test (BAT), which detect autoantibodies against IgE. Elevated levels of inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), interleukins, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) have been reported in urticaria patients. The Urticaria Activity Score (UAS7) is a questionnaire-based tool that evaluates the severity of spontaneous urticaria based on pruritus and wheal frequency. Treatment of urticaria focuses on symptom relief. The first-line therapy is H1 antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, cetirizine, and other similar agents. Some patients may require higher doses of antihistamines for adequate symptom control, which are generally well-tolerated. If first-line treatments fail, second-line options include omalizumab and cyclosporine. Omalizumab has shown efficacy in various urticaria subtypes, including solar urticaria, cold urticaria, cholinergic urticaria, urticarial vasculitis, and symptomatic dermatographic urticaria. Alternative treatments include dapsone, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, colchicine, methotrexate, intravenous gamma globulin, plasmapheresis, corticosteroids, H2 antagonists, and leukotriene antagonists. Specific treatments may be recommended for certain urticaria subtypes based on clinical studies. Primary prevention involves identifying and avoiding triggers that provoke wheal formation. Common triggers include food allergens, cold temperatures, and physical stimuli. Patients are advised to avoid tight-fitting clothing and hot baths immediately following an urticaria episode.
